brief_data.hook:
You finally get the chance you wanted, and a small voice says, "They'll find out you're not that good."
Learn how to answer impostor thoughts with three pieces of evidence and one sentence that owns your work.
brief_data.summary: Days before presenting her pipeline to Mark's team in Seattle, Sena types "Basically a faster spreadsheet" under the title of her first slide, and a small voice says everyone will find out. Daniel shares a systematic review by Bravata and colleagues of 62 studies, where impostor feelings ranged from 9% to 82% depending on how they were measured, and Basima Tewfik's research, where people with workplace impostor thoughts were rated as better with others but had lower self-esteem. He tells the story of underselling himself to his VP and the "Receipts" file he has kept ever since, and they compare Japanese modesty, which listeners quietly add back, with US meetings, where small words are taken literally. Today's challenge: write down three pieces of evidence of your own work: a number, a result, or something someone said to you.

brief_data.hook:
A request arrives late at night, and your reply already says "Of course! Happy to help!" even though you know it will take three days you don't have.
Learn how to say no in a few clear sentences, with a real alternative, and keep the relationship warm.
brief_data.summary: Two days before her first presentation to Mark's team, a late-night Slack message asks Sena for a twelve-month breakdown that would take three days, and her "Of course!" reply is waiting on the send button. Daniel shares research by Givi and Kirk, where people who said no overestimated how upset the other person would be, and by Zauberman and Lynch, where people expected more free time next month than today. He tells the story of the one-line no that came back to him six months later, and they compare soft Japanese refusals like "it's a little difficult" with the US view that a late no hurts trust more than an early one. Today's challenge: say no to one request today and offer one alternative with it.
